defaults.permitted_development: Across Cornwall, domestic heat pumps are usually easiest on the planning permission route when the unit stays compact, sits discreetly, and can show a clean noise and neighbour-amenity story under the English planning system. More exposed elevations and open views can make siting and screening feel more sensitive than a simple compact-unit assumption suggests.

rules.height_rules: Bulky housings, stacked equipment or extra height and visual prominence can make a heat pump feel more like external plant than a modest domestic installation.
rules.depth_rules: Projection from the wall or building line matters because exposed units and screens can quickly look more intrusive than a tighter, building-hugging installation.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary siting and noise are usually the first planning pressure points for heat pumps across Cornwall, especially where the unit sits near neighbours or a quiet garden edge.
rules.roof_rules: Roof siting is rarely the easiest heat pump route across Cornwall. Roof-mounted plant, visible pipe runs and brackets usually need a closer look than a compact ground- or wall-level installation that keeps the main roofscape clear.
rules.materials_rules: Well-scaled screening and restrained finishes usually work better than oversized housings that create a second visual problem around the plant.

rules.materials_rules: Restrained screening and a tidy finish usually help a heat pump scheme in Cornwall far more than heavy enclosures that add visual bulk.

restrictions.conservation_area: Heat pumps in conservation areas within Cornwall often face a closer review where the unit or its screening is visible from public viewpoints.
restrictions.listed_building: Heat pump installations on or around listed buildings in Cornwall usually need a more careful planning and heritage consent assessment.
